Even apart from the Administrative Procedure Act this Court has for 
more than four decades emphasized that the formulation of procedures was 
basically to be left within the discretion of the agencies to which Congress 
had confided the responsibility for substantive judgments. * * *
* * * [T]he Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit * * * 
seriously misread or misapphed this statutory and decisional law. * * *
Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, 42 U.S.C. § 2011 et seq.^ the 
[Nuclear Regulatory] Commission was given broad regulatory authority 
over the development of nuclear energy. Under the terms of the Act, a 
utility seeking to construct and operate a nuclear power plant must obtain 
a separate permit or license at both the construction and the operation 
stage of the project. In order to obtain the construction permit, the utihty 
must file a preliminary safety analysis report, an environmental report, 
and certain information regarding the antitrust impheations of the 
proposed project. This appheation then undergoes exhaustive review by the 
Commission’s staff and by the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards 
(ACRS), a group of distinguished experts in the field of atomic energy. Both

In December 1967, after the mandatory adjudicatory hearing and 
necessary review, the Commission granted petitioner Vermont Yankee a 
permit to build a nuclear power plant in Vernon, Vt. Thereafter, Vermont 
Yankee apphed for an operating hcense. Respondent Natural Resources 
Defense Council (NRDC) objected to the granting of a hcense, however, and 
therefore a hearing on the appheation commenced on August 10, 1971. 
Excluded from consideration at the hearings, over NRDC’s objection, was 
the issue of the environmental effects of operations to reprocess fuel or 
dispose of wastes resulting from the reprocessing operations. This ruling 
was affirmed by the Appeal Board in June 1972.
